messages.author: 760d13932202d6cf
messages.subject: SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for point.domain
parts:
Hi,

I want to include physical boundaries while using inla.mesh.create.helper(...,point.domain=borders).
In Cameletti et al (2012) I see that object 'borders' is a data.frame with 2 columns corresponding to coords x and y. I was just wondering if there is a way to use SpatialPolygonsDataFrame class without conversion.  If not, is there a smart/easy way of extracting coordinates.

Many thanks,
Olga

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for point.domain
parts:
On 20/02/13 16:01, Olga Lyashevska wrote:
> I want to include physical boundaries while using
> inla.mesh.create.helper(...,point.domain=borders).
> In Cameletti et al (2012) I see that object 'borders' is a data.frame
> with 2 columns corresponding to coords x and y. I was just wondering
> if there is a way to use SpatialPolygonsDataFrame class without
> conversion. If not, is there a smart/easy way of extracting coordinates.

Hi,

there is experimental support for converting from SpatialPolygons to the
kind of information needed by inla.mesh.create.helper:

The function
inla.sp2segment
handles conversion from Polygon, Polygons, and SpatialPolygons.
You'll likely need to extract the SpatialPolygons slot call "polygons"
from your SpatialPolygonsDataFrame to use it, but I haven't tested that.

Technically, this is not "without conversion", but technically such a
conversion _must_ happen somewhere in the code, and currently it needs
to be done on the user side.

Finn

Yes, this can work for simple polygons. inla.sp2segment handles the
multi-polygon case (e.g. regions with "holes") and sets (or tries to
set) the orientation appropriate for inla (boundary = counter-clockwise,
interior hole = clockwise).

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for point.domain
parts:
There is an example using the Finn's inla.sp2segment() function:

### get the NC map
require(spdep)
nc.fl <- system.file("etc/shapes/sids.shp", package="spdep")[1]
nc.sids <- readShapePoly(nc.fl, ID="FIPSNO",
proj4s=CRS("+proj=longlat +ellps=clrk66"))

### reduce the number of polygons (get the border of NC, by union)
require(rgeos)
nc.border <- unionSpatialPolygons(nc.sids, rep(1, nrow(nc.sids)))

### get the mesh using the NC border
require(INLA)
nc.boundary <- inla.sp2segment(nc.border)
nc.mesh <- inla.mesh.create(boundary=nc.boundary,
refine=list(max.edge=0.2))

### visualize
par(mar=c(0,0,0,0))
plot(nc.border)
plot(nc.mesh, add=TRUE)

best,
Elias.

parts:
I want to thank everyone for the help!

I am still trying different options to account for a physical boundary of my region.
Now I ended up with two possibilities, and I do not quite understand in which way they differ.

So if I want to include a boundary of the region I have (at least) these two options:

Option 1. 
Follow Cameletti (page 15) and create object 'borders' which is a data.frame.
I created this object from a spdf like so:

borders.shp<-readShapePoly("./borders.shp")
borders<-as.data.frame(borders.shp@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords)
mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(data@coords,points.domain=borders,max.edge=c(0.5,2), plot.delay=1)

Now, when I use this object to specify point.domain, my mesh is having a hard time (plot.delay=1 nicely shows the process) and after some time and many tiny triangles it results in 'Error in fmesher read(prefix,"manifold"). 
I saw a ticket for this issue, is it still a problem or is it me doing something wrong?

My area is approximately 200km long, where I have a 500x500m grid of sampling locations. Should I be specifying max.edge as something in the range of my sampling grid (e.g 500 m)?

Option 2.
Follow suggestion from Finn and Elias and use inla.mesh.segment to create boundary. 
When I try to follow an example, here:

require(spdep)
borders.shp<-readShapePoly("./borders.shp")
require(rgeos)
#Do I need this line? I have just one polygon?
nc.borders <- unionSpatialPolygons(borders.shp, rep(1, nrow(borders.shp)))
require(INLA)
nc.boundary <- inla.sp2segment(nc.borders)
nc.mesh <- inla.mesh.create(boundary=nc.boundary, refine=list(max.edge=0.2),     plot.delay=1)
# visualize
par(mar=c(0,0,0,0))
plot(borders.shp)
#Here I get the error
plot(nc.mesh, add=TRUE)

Error in cbind(mesh$graph$tv[t.sub, c(1:3, 1), drop = FALSE], NA) :

What is the difference between these two options? According to Cameletti, option 2 would generate a much too detailed boundary. Is that all?

Many thanks,
Olga

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for point.domain
parts:
On 21/02/13 16:28, Olga Lyashevska wrote:
> Now I ended up with two possibilities, and I do not quite understand
> in which way they differ.

Option 1 merely says that the mesh should cover the data coordinates as
well as the border coordinates, but doesn't set the boundary equal to
the border. Option 2 (disregarding the error) tries to set the mesh
boundary equal to the border.

The issue with your code in Option 1 is precisely what you guessed, that
max.edge needs to be adjusted to match the units of your coordinates.
Are they in metres or kilometres? max.edge should be specified in the
same units.

In Option 2, try replacing the inla.sp2segment code with this:

nc.boundary =
inla.mesh.segment(borders.shp@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords)

and see if that makes a difference. I don't recall getting your error
message.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for point.domain
parts:
> What is the difference between these two options? According to
Cameletti, option 2 would generate a much too detailed boundary. Is that
all?

...and yes, if your boundary has fine detail, that will happen.
However, you can specify a "cutoff" parameter, that makes the
triangulation avoid adding points close together. This will apply to
both data locations and boundary points, and is usually a good idea for
irregularly spaced points, since it avoids clusters of tiny triangles.

Finn

You can see here http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/case-studies/Cameletti2012/run_model.R
that borders are obtained by the following:

So now I obtain a matrix and plug it in as a points domain.

After all, I manage to obtain a mesh (which still needs to be fine-tuned) and it works both on data frame and matrix.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: SpatialPolygonsDataFrame for point.domain
parts: For the benefit of the group/list, here's a quick summary of the solution to the problem.

Error in cbind(mesh$graph$tv[t.sub, c(1:3, 1), drop = FALSE], NA) :
  subscript out of bounds

This error was a secondary error, due to trying to plot an empty mesh.
The mesh was empty because the shape data used to define the boundary was self-intersecting.
Since the triangulation software cannot deal with self-intersecting boundary edges (when a closed polygon is self-intersecting, "inside" and "outside"  is not well-defined), that left a gap in the boundary, leading the whole domain to be classified as "outside", and hence removed.

In this case the self-intersection was a very small loop, and could be ignored by setting the "cutoff" parameter in inla.mesh.create to a distance larger than the size of the loop.

As a side-effect of debugging this I've looked through the boundary handling code, and corrected some old annoying deficiencies.   The inla.sp2segment() function(s) will, from the next package update, support conversion from Polygon,Polygons,SpatialPolygons and SpatialPolygonsDataFrame.  inla.mesh.create.helper will handle boundaries without the user having to adjust 2D coordinates to 3D.

Finn
